hook_text: Seven hundred years ago, in the middle of the Sahara, there was a town where the houses were built of salt.
clip_script: It was called Taghaza, and a traveller named Ibn Battuta saw it in 1352: walls of salt blocks, roofs of camel skin, and workers digging slabs of salt out of the ground. Why would anyone live there? Because south of the desert, in West Africa, salt was precious. People in the heat sweat it out and need it to live. Food goes bad without it. And West Africa had little salt but plenty of something else: gold. So camels carried salt south and gold north, and for centuries much of the gold in Europe's coins came from West Africa. The kingdom of Mali sat in the middle, taxing it all, and became one of the richest places on Earth.
